full_judgment:
BB Roy Choudhury J: This Rule arises with reference to an ejahar which was lodged with Paba Police Station by the Anti-corruption Inspector against the accused-petitioners u/s 467/468 and some other sections of the Penal Code.

2. The allegations against the petitioners were to the effect that with a view to cheating one Shamsuddin, the Petitioners in collusion with each other forged a document and used the same in Mutation Case No. 1606/9-1/77-78 dated 25-5-78 before the Revenue Officer. Following a charge-sheet submitted thereupon, a criminal case being DGR Case No. 19 of 1980 was ultimately started against the petitioners in the Court of the Additional District Magistrate, Rajshahi u/s 468/471 of the Penal Code. But on 24-6-84, the date fixed for appearance of the accused opposite-parties and framing of charge, the learned Additional District Magistrate discharged both the petitioners being of the view that the Revenue Officer holding mutation proceeding must be treated as a Court within the meaning of section 195 (1) (c) of the Code of Criminal Procedure and there being no complaint from him the taking of cognizance in the case was illegal. The learned Sessions Judge, Rajshahi was then moved in the matter by the State in Criminal Motion No. 222 of 1984. He took the view that a Revenue Officer could not be treated as a Presiding Officer of a Court and as such no complaint u/s 195 (1)(c) of the Code of Criminal Procedure was necessary in the case. Accordingly, by an order dated 21-1-85, the learned Sessions Judge set-aside the order of discharge and directed the learned Additional District Magistrate to proceed with the case according to law. This Rule has now been obtained by the accused-petitioners against the said order of the learned Sessions Judge.

2. None appears for the petitioners in support of the Rule while the learned Deputy Attorney-General appearing on behalf of the opposite-party supports the order of the learned Sessions Judge. He submits that the Revenue Officer holding mutation proceeding does not act as a Court within the meaning of section 195 (1)(c) of the Code of Criminal Procedure and, therefore, there was no bar for the Magistrate in taking cognizance of the case in the absence of any complaint from him.

<u>3. Section 195 of the Code of Criminal Procedure puts restriction on the general power conferred upon all courts of the Magistrate by section 190 of the Code of Criminal Procedure to take cognizance of offences. Relevant portion of section 195 of the Code with which we are concerned in this case is reproduced below:</u>

<u>(I) No Court shall take cognizance—</u>

<u>(a)  ................................................</u>

<u>(b)  ................................................</u>

<u>(c) of any offence described in section 463 or punishable under section 471, section 475 or section 476 of the same Code, when such offence is alleged to have been committed by a party to any proceeding in any Court in respect of a document produced or given in evidence in such proceeding, except on the complaint in writing of such Court, or of some other Court to which court is sub-ordinate.</u>

<u>(2) In clauses (b) and (c) of sub-section (1), the term "Court" includes a Civil Revenue or Criminal Court, but does not include a Registrar or Sub-Registrar under the Registration Act, 1908.</u>

<u>It provides that when an offence specified in section 195(1) (c) of the Criminal Procedure Code appears to have been committed by a party to any proceeding in any Court in respect of a document produced or given in evidence in such a proceeding, no Court is competent to take cognizance of such an offence except on the complaint in writing of the Court concerned or some other Court to which it is sub-ordinate. This provision thus requires that without a complaint in writing of the Court concerned or some other Court to which it is sub-ordinate no prosecution for an offence mentioned in clause (c) of sub-section (1) of section 195 of the Code can be taken cognizance of.</u>

4. In the instant case, if the Revenue officer who held the mutation proceeding is found to be a Court, the taking of cognizance of the offence by the Magistrate, in the absence of any complainant from him, would be held to be illegal. But if it is found otherwise, the impugned order must be up-held. The only question that arises for determination in this Rule, therefore, is whether a Revenue Officer dealing with mutation case constitutes a Court within the meaning of section 195(1)(c) of the Criminal Procedure Code.

<u>5. There is no definition of the expression "Court" in the Code of Criminal Procedure, but it is provided in section 4(2) of the Code that "all words and expressions used herein and defined in the Penal Code, and not herein before defined, shall be deemed to have the meanings respectively attributed to them by that Code!' The only Court which is defined in the Penal Code is a "Court of Justice" which denotes a Judge who is empowered to act judicially alone or a body of Judges which is empowered by law to act judicially. Section 19 of the Penal Code declares that a Judge denotes not only a person who is officially designated as such, but also every person who is empowered by law to give in any legal proceeding, civil or criminal, a definitive judgment, or a judgment which, if not appealed against, would be definitive, or would acquire that character when confirmed by some other authority, or who is one of a body of persons by law to give such a judgment. This definition is some-what wide but section 195 Criminal Procedure Code has made the provision sufficiently wider to include all civil, criminal or revenue Courts.</u>

6. There being no exhaustive definition of Court in any statute, the question what a Court is gave rise to a good deal of judicial controversies. In a long series of decisions the superior Courts of this Sub-continent pointed out the essential characteristics that invest a person or a body of persons with the character of a Court.

<u>7. In the case of: Bharat Bank Ltd. vs Employees of Bharat Bank Ltd. AIR 1950 SC 188 the Supreme Court of India considered the essential sine qua non of a Court and held as follows:</u>

<u>"As pointed out in Halsbury's Laws of England, the word "Court" originally meant the King's Palace but subsequently acquired the meaning of (1) a Palace where justice was administered, and (2) the person or persons who administer it. In the Evidence Act, it is defined as including all Judges and Magistrates and all persons except arbitrators legally authorised to take evidence. This definition is by no means exhaustive and has been framed only for the purpose of the Act. There can be no doubt that to be a Court, the person or persons who constitute it must be entrusted with judicial functions, that is, of deciding litigated questions according to law. However, by agreement, between parties arbitrators may be called upon to exercise judicial powers and to decide a dispute according to law but that would not make the arbitrators a Court. It appears to me that before a person or persons can be said to constitute a Court, it must be held that they derive their powers from the state and are exercising the judicial powers of the State."</u>

8. The precise meaning of judicial power was given by Griffith, CJ in the case of Huddart Parker & Co. vs Moorhead, 8 CLR 330 at page 357 where he said: I am of opinion that the words 'judicial power' as used in section 71 of the Constitution mean the power which every sovereign authority must of necessity have to decide controversies between its subjects, or between itself and its subjects, whether the rights relate to life, liberty or property. The exercise of this power does not begin until some tribunal which has power to give a binding and authoritative decision (whether subject to appeal or not) is called upon to take action." This definition was accepted by the Privy Council as the best definition of judicial power in the case of Shell Co. of Australia Ltd. vs Federal Commissioner of Taxation, 1931 AC 276.

<u>9. The principle expressed in AIR 1950 SC 188 was reiterated by the Supreme Court of India in a good number of its subsequent decisions. Suffice it to refer to the case of Brajnandan Sinha vs Jyoti Narain, PLD 1956 SC (Ind) 65, where their Lordships laid down the essential tests of a Court in the following terms:</u>

<u>"It is clear, therefore, that in order to constitute a Court is the strict sense of the term, an essential condition is that the Court should have, apart from having some of the trappings of a judicial tribunal, power to give a decision or a definitive judgment which has finality and authoritativeness which are the essential tests of judicial pronouncement.'</u>

10. In the case of Muhammad Saeed vs Election Petitions Tribunal, West Pakistan etc. 9 DLR (SC) 139 ; 1957 (SC) (Pak) 91 at page 116 Cornelius J pointed out the following indicia of a Court :

"(1) to be a Court, the person or persons constituting such Court, must be entrusted with judicial functions, i.e., of deciding litigated questions according to law:

(2) such person or persons must derive the power of so deciding questions, from the State, and therefore will be exercising the judicial powers of the State ; and

(3) the appointment of the person or persons constituting a Court should be by the Government ; these persons should receive payment for their services exclusively out of Government funds and they should not be liable to removal by any authority other than the Government."

<u>11. This Court had also the occasion to analyse the different attributes of a Court in several decisions. In the case of IDBP vs M/s. Master Industries (1974) 26 DLR 157 and in the case of Shamsul Huq Sikder vs Election Tribunal & others, (1975) 27 DLR 388 it was laid down that "the exercise of judicial power of the State is the determining factor for investing a body with the character of a Court and that a Tribunal exercising a judicial power does not mean merely that it is acting with fairness and impartiality on a proper consideration of all relevant materials after giving an opportunity to all contending parties to present their respective cases. In order that exercise of judicial power or acting judicially may be a sign of acting as a Court, it must be acting as a part of the judicial machinery of the State, charged with the duty of determining the rights of one subject against another or a question of right between the subject and State and discharging its function according to established form of judicial procedure."</u>

12. A tribunal is not always furnished with the trappings of a Court, nor such trappings make its action judicial. The character of the action it performs and the nature of the right on which it operates determine whether its action is judicial of ministerial. Whenever, a question, therefore, arises as to whether an office or tribunal is a Court as distinguished from a quasi judicial or administrative tribunal it is necessary to decide whether having regard to the provisions of the relevant Act, it possesses the essential attributes of a Court, as indicated above.

13. Mutation proceedings are done under the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and the Rules framed thereunder. So let us now examine the provisions of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and the Rules framed thereunder, insofar as those relate to the powers and duties of a Revenue Officer and the procedure he follows in mutating one's name in the record-of rights.

<u>14. Section 143 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act provides, inter alia, that the record-of-right prepared or revised shall be maintained up to date in the prescribed manner under Part IV, or under chapter XVII by correcting clerical mistakes and by incorporating the changes on account of (a) the mutation of names as a result of transfer or inheritance.</u>

<u>15. Chapter VI of the Tenancy Rules, 1955 consists of rules 22-25 of which rules 22-24 relate to mutation proceedings. Relevant portions of the said rules are reproduced be, low:</u>

<u>22. Duties of Tahshilder: (1) The Tahshilder or Patwari shall be primarily responsible for reporting promptly to the Revenue Officer immediately superior to him (apparent clerical mistakes in the record-of rights,) all charges in the owner-ship of land, all cases of alluvion, diluvion and reformation of land and the particulars or unsettled lands, in his area...................</u>

<u>(2) In the cases of succession, intestate or testamentary the report shall contain the names and addresses of all heirs and their respective shares and nature of interests according to the law of inheritance applicable to the deceased or according to the terms of the testament, as the case may be, and also the description of the holding or holdings they have inherited. The report shall also state, if any, area of land inherited by any heir if acquirable under section 91 of the Act.</u>

<u>(3) In the case of alluvion, diluvion and reformation of land the report shall state its nature, area and location and, in the case of reformation or accretion, also the Khatian number of the holding to which it relates and the area which the raiyat concerned is entitled to possess under the provisions of section 86 or section 87 of the Act, as the case may be.</u>

<u>23. Duties of Revenue Officers :- (1) The Revenue Officer shall, if he is vested with necessary powers in this behalf under the Act, incorporate, and if he is not vested with such powers, send up proposals to the officer vested with such powers for incorporating necessary changes in the record of rights—</u>

<u>(a) When mutation of names is allowed as a result of inheritance either on the report of the Tahshilder under rule 22 or on the application of the heirs or otherwise;</u>

<u>(b) When mutation of names is made as a result of transfer on receipt of the notice of transfer under section 89 of the Act;</u>

<u>(2) Before sending any report under this rule, the Revenue Officer shall satisfy himself about its correctness and for this purpose he may make such enquiries and take such evidence as he thinks fit.</u>

<u>24. Duties of officers entrusted with the work of maintaining the record-of-rights :- (1) Subject to the provision of sub-rule (2), the officer entrusted with the work of maintaining the record-of-rights shall promptly incorporate therein all changes reported to him under rule 23.</u>

<u>(2) Before incorporating any change in the record-of-rights, the officer shall carefully examine the report on the basis of which the change is to be made and shall satisfy himself about its correctness and for that purpose he shall follow such procedure and take such action as may be directed by the Board of Revenue.</u>

<u>On an analysis of the rule in the light of the tests indicated above we are unable to characterise the functions assigned to a Revenue Officer as judicial functions. Under the rules a Revenue Officer is invested with the power of mutation of names but he has to act on the report of a Tahshilder. The primary responsibility lies with the Tahshilder to report to the Revenue Officer when any change in the ownership of land takes place. Upon this report the Revenue officer incorporates the necessary change in the record of-rights. It he is not vested with the requisite power in that behalf he sends up a proposal to the officer vested with such power for incorporating the necessary changes in the record-of rights when mutation of names is allowed as a result of inheritance or transfer. Before sending the proposal, the Revenue Officer may, however, make enquiries and take such evidence as he may think fit so as to satisfy himself as to the correctness of the report. The enquiry he makes appears to be an enquiry conducted by an up-to-date record-of-rights. He does not decide anything by a definitive judgment. The decision he gives is subject to the determination of the right by a civil Court. The mere fact that such an officer has been invested with the power to take evidence in course of an enquiry in a mutation proceeding does not make him a Court. His order of mutation is "merely an executive order" as held by a Division Bench of the Dhaka High Court in the case of SM Lutfullah vs Bibi Badrunnessa, (1968) 20 DLR (Dhaka) 1019. In view of the above it is patent that a Revenue Officer holding mutation proceeding does not act as a Court within the meaning of section 195(1)(c) Criminal Procedure Code.</u>

<u>17. The view we have taken finds, support from the decision of the Privy Council in the case of Nirman Singh vs Thakurlal Rudra Protap Narain-Singh, AIR "1926 PC 100. In that case their Lordships held that mutation proceedings, is "in the nature of fiscal-inquiry instituted in the interest of the State for the purpose of ascertaining which of the several claimants for the occupation of certain denominations of immoveable property may be put into occupation of it with greater confidence that the revenue for it will be paid" and that it was an error to suppose that such proceedings are "judicial proceedings in which the title to and the proprietary rights in immoveable property are determined."</u>

18. Relying on this decision a Division Bench of the High Court of West Pakistan held in the case of Malik Patch Khan vs Nazibullah Khan, (1957) 9 DLR, WP (Lahore) 40 that "a Revenue Officer when dealing with a mutation, either originally or in appeal does not constitute a Court."

In the case of Mst Thari vs Mohammad PLD 1973 SC 619 the Supreme Court of Pakistan while dealing with the question whether a Mutation Officer is a Court within the meaning of section 195 of the Criminal Procedure Code observed as follows:

It is idle to suggest that Mutation Officer is a Court."

<u>19. We are in full agreement, with the view expressed in the aforesaid decision. We are, therefore, of the opinion that a Revenue Officer dealing with a mutation proceeding under the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and the Rule framed there-under does not constitute a Court. Since we have found that a Revenue Officer acting under Rule 23 of the Tenancy Rule is not a Court, it is needless for us to dilate on the question whether he is a civil, criminal or Revenue Court.</u>

<u>For the reason stated above we are of the view that the allegations in this criminal case do not attract the provisions of sections 195 (1)(c) Criminal Procedure Code. Accordingly we find no error in the order of the learned Sessions Judge.</u>

In the result, the Rule is discharged.

End.
